subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Tea and Chinese Medicine
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Tea and Chinese Medicine.

hook.text: In traditional Chinese medicine, different teas are prescribed for different body types and ailments.

buildup.text: Green tea is considered 'cooling.' It's recommended for people who run hot—with red faces and restlessness.

discovery.text: Roasted oolong and aged pu-erh are 'warming.' They're prescribed for cold constitutions—pale skin, poor circulation.

twist.text: This system has no strong evidence by Western standards, yet 1.5 billion people consider it common knowledge.

climax.text: Modern research is exploring whether TCM tea prescriptions have biochemical basis—early results are promising for some claims.

punchline.text: Ancient wisdom, modern questions. Tea as medicine isn't settled yet.

quiz.question: How does traditional Chinese medicine classify green tea?
options: As a cooling tea for people who run hot

details.summary: Traditional Chinese medicine classifies teas by their warming or cooling properties. Green tea is considered cooling and suited for summer, while heavily oxidized teas like pu-erh are warming. Tea is prescribed alongside herbs to balance the body's qi.
details.whyItMatters: The medicinal framework gives tea a purpose beyond flavor in Chinese culture. Understanding it explains why Chinese people choose different teas for different seasons and conditions.
takeaways: Chinese medicine classifies teas as cooling or warming
Green tea is cooling; pu-erh and black teas are warming
People choose teas to balance their body's energy or qi

faq.question: How do the cooling and warming properties work?
faq.answer: In traditional Chinese medicine, cooling teas like green and white are recommended for people with excess heat or during summer. Warming teas like pu-erh and black tea are suited for cold weather or people with cold constitutions. Oolong is considered neutral. The framework is about balance.

faq.question: Do modern Chinese people still choose tea based on these principles?
faq.answer: Many do, especially older generations and those in traditional communities. Even urbanized Chinese often observe basic guidelines like avoiding cold green tea in winter. The principles are embedded in cultural practice even for people who do not explicitly follow traditional Chinese medicine.
